ImageDescription.value:
Although the soft spring days of “April in Paris” have been famously memorialized in song, travel ads wax eloquent about the equally wonderful days of April in Florida. One travel site states “this tropical state has excellent weather year-round, but April, in particular, is a nice blend of sunny, warm days without being oppressively hot”. Another more evocatively raves, “the best time of year for dry weather and buckets of sunshine”.

On April 22, 2019, the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) on board NASA’s Aqua satellite acquired a true-color image of a bucketful-of-sun spring day across Florida.

The dark greens mark areas of heavy vegetation, primarily found in parks and preserves. Such areas are fairly representative of the natural flora of the state prior to the heavy influx of agriculture, industry, and residents seeking sunny, pleasant living. Lighter areas of green and tan mark agricultural regions, both crops and pasturage. In April, the commercial harvest nears its peak and includes bell peppers, blueberries, cabbage, cantaloupe, carrot, celery, cucumber, grapefruit, guava, lettuce, mushroom, orange, papaya, peaches, peanut, potato, radish, snap bean, spinach, squash strawberry, sweet corn, tangerine, tomato and watermelon.

Another perennial crop, housing and habitation, can also be seen in the image—areas of heavy human activity, such as highways and cities, appear gray. Jacksonville can be seen as a large, mostly gray area near the Atlantic Ocean coastline (east coast) in the north of the image, and the gray continues nearly unbroken along the entire east coast, which is a very popular place to live and vacation. Inland, near the center of the image, the gray area is Orlando, a favored tourist spot. On the Gulf Coast (west), Clearwater, St. Petersburg and Tampa cluster around Tampa Bay. Greenish sediment hugs the coast near these cities, from north of Tampa Bay to well south of it. The shiny silver color seen on Lake Okeechobee, in the south, and over the southern Atlantic Ocean is an artifact called “sunglint”. This is an optical effect caused by the mirror-like reflection of sunlight off the water surface directly back at the satellite sensor.
